chapters.title: Failure gallery, Failure 3: The three-eyed cyclopses
Prompt engineering, Common failure modes and fixes

diagnoses.diagnosis: The model is re-drawing the face every frame with nothing pinning it down. Long clips, moving cameras, and crowded frames all give the face room to wander. Consistency is the floor, not the ceiling, no concept survives visible morphing.
fix: Shorten the clip (3 seconds is the rescue length).
Lock the start frame: generate or approve a still first, then animate from it.
Static camera for the rescue pass, remove camera motion as a variable.
Add an exclusion block to every prompt: no morphing faces, no shifting features, no extra limbs.
If it still morphs, regenerate from the locked frame. Do not extend a morphing clip.
diagnoses.what_you_see: Features slide, warp, or rearrange during a single clip, the face at second 4 is not the face at second 1.

chapters.title: Directing performance, Casting the face
Prompt engineering, Common failure modes and fixes

diagnoses.diagnosis: You are re-describing the character in every prompt instead of using an identity system. Each description is a new roll of the dice. A face that drifts 5% between shots reads as a bad performance even when the acting is fine.
fix: Lock the face anchor: one approved close-up, never re-run the base portrait.
Restate the same three locked traits verbatim in every prompt, or use an identity system (Soul ID and equivalents) instead of descriptions.
Keep a library of approved frames and use them as start frames.
State changes (dirt, wounds, tears) are masked integrations in post, never re-generations.
Compare each output to the reference before accepting; reject on any trait change.
diagnoses.symptom: Character looks different from shot to shot
diagnoses.what_you_see: Same character, different person: jawline, eyes, or age shift between cuts. The audience reads it as a stranger, not a bad take.

chapters.title: Failure gallery, Failure 5: Dead, glassy eyes
Directing performance, Give the eyes a job
Directing performance, The dead-eyes checklist

diagnoses.diagnosis: There is no eyeline written. Nine times out of ten, a dead performance is a missing eyeline, not a model limitation. Dead, glassy eyes are never fixed with lighting, they are fixed by giving the eyes a job.
fix: Name the eyeline target per beat: who or what the eyes are on, and when they move.
Use eye verbs, avert, hold, search, track, instead of emotional adjectives.
Cut to the listener: in dialogue, the listener's eyes do half the acting.
Run the dead-eyes checklist: microsaccades, the Duchenne smile (real joy crinkles the eyes), natural asymmetry, pupillary response.
Teach the machine to be flawed to be accepted, hyper-symmetrical faces read as averaged and artificial.
sources: ONEIRIC production brief (tig-acting-task, CINEDANCE block order)
Uncanny-valley aliveness markers (Fernando Andrade, Medium, Feb 2026)
diagnoses.what_you_see: The fastest tell of an undirected AI performance: eyes fixed on nothing, no life behind them, the "soul blindness" stare.

chapters.title: Prompt engineering, Common failure modes and fixes
Directing performance, Ration the close-up

diagnoses.diagnosis: The model is averaging skin detail at a resolution where faces are a few dozen pixels. Wides are the weakest link for faces, the model fills the gap with smooth, waxy interpolation.
fix: Punch in: regenerate the problem shot as a medium close-up with natural skin texture, pores, and catchlights written into the prompt.
If the wide is otherwise good, composite the close face over it in post.
Spend close-ups at emotional peaks anyway, that is where the audience looks hardest and where the model fails most visibly.
Wides and mediums carry the rest of the scene; they read as confident filmmaking.
diagnoses.what_you_see: Skin looks airbrushed and artificial, especially in wide shots, the "video-game cutscene" sheen.

chapters.title: Failure gallery, Failure 1: The subtle-acting collapse
Directing performance, Direct, don't describe
Directing performance, One feeling per shot

diagnoses.diagnosis: You described a feeling and the model gave you the stock version of it. Models cannot render "devastated", they average toward a pleasant blank. Emotion labels produce stock expressions instead of felt ones.
fix: Stop describing feelings; direct playable tactics: "she looks devastated" becomes "she is trying not to cry in front of him, jaw set, eyes on the door."
One tactic per shot; the turn happens in the cut, not inside the clip.
The reaction shot is your best friend, AI renders listening better than it renders complex feeling.
Break emotional turns into separate shots: AI can hold one tactic for 4 to 8 seconds, not an arc.
sources: ONEIRIC tig-acting-task rule, direct, don't describe
diagnoses.symptom: Emotion reads as blank or stock
diagnoses.what_you_see: "She looks devastated" renders as a pleasant neutral. Micro-expressions collapse; the audience reads mannequin theater.

chapters.title: Failure gallery, Failure 4: Flat acting at $2M
Directing performance, Restraint by default
Directing performance, One feeling per shot

diagnoses.diagnosis: Licensed likeness gives you a consistent face; it does not give you acting. Direction is the fix at every budget, The Cully Hill Boys had $2M and mapped likenesses and still got flagged for flat, mis-prompted acting.
fix: Apply the same discipline as a zero-budget short: tactics not emotions, eyelines per beat, restraint by default.
Let the listener's reaction shot sell the line.
If the scene's entire job is one human feeling something complicated, shoot or voice it for real and transform with AI, the hybrid answer scales from shorts to features.
Default to restraint: underplayed beats read as intentional; overplayed beats read as synthetic.
sources: The Verge / Semafor reviews of The Cully Hill Boys
diagnoses.symptom: Flat acting despite a good likeness
diagnoses.what_you_see: The face is consistent and recognizable, but nothing lands, weak character interactions, line readings with no weight.

chapters.title: Prompt engineering, Common failure modes and fixes
Prompt engineering, The exclusion block

diagnoses.diagnosis: Hands are high-complexity geometry the model guesses at. Small, fast-moving, or occluded hands are where the guesswork shows first.
fix: Keep hands out of frame or still for the generation; add motion in post if needed.
Exclude deformed hands explicitly: add "no extra fingers, no melting hands" to the exclusion block of every prompt.
Crop in post, reframing is cheaper than regenerating.
The first-short checkpoint rule: every prompt carries an exclusion block ("no morphing faces, no extra fingers, no text"). No exclusions, no generation.
diagnoses.what_you_see: Extra fingers, fused digits, hands that melt into props, the classic AI tell.

chapters.title: Prompt engineering, Common failure modes and fixes

diagnoses.diagnosis: The model is re-solving texture and fine detail every frame with no temporal anchor. Busy backgrounds multiply the problem, every leaf and brick is another chance to boil.
fix: Regenerate, flicker is often a bad seed, not a bad prompt.
Simplify the background: avoid overly busy textures behind the subject.
Stabilize in post: temporal denoising and deflicker passes exist for exactly this.
Shorter clips flicker less; the rescue length is 3 seconds.
diagnoses.what_you_see: Surfaces shimmer and crawl between frames, fabric, foliage, and brickwork boil instead of sitting still.

chapters.title: Prompt engineering, Common failure modes and fixes
Cinematic language, Camera movements

diagnoses.diagnosis: The camera move was decoration, not motivation. Unmotivated moves drift because the prompt never said what the move was for, so the model improvised.
fix: Name one explicit camera move per shot, one motivated move beats two unmotivated ones.
Pin an end frame: knowing where the camera lands kills drift.
Shorten the duration; drift compounds over time.
Rule: every movement needs a purpose. Ask what the move reveals or withholds.
diagnoses.what_you_see: The camera slides, pans, or floats without purpose, movement that reveals nothing and withholds nothing.

chapters.title: Prompt engineering, Per-shot discipline
Prompt engineering, The exclusion block

diagnoses.diagnosis: The prompt asked for too much. One shot = one fully self-contained prompt; the model has no memory of your last clip and limited attention for your current one. Too many actions in five seconds means none of them land.
fix: One action per clip. Don't ask for three beats in one generation.
Restate the full premise every time, the model has no memory of the last shot.
Keep the frame uncrowded: fewer subjects means fewer failure modes.
Prefer image-to-video for control: generate the still, approve it, then animate.
Write island prompts: everything re-stated, every time.
diagnoses.what_you_see: You asked for three specific things; the clip delivers one of them, or none. The more the prompt asks, the less it gets.

chapters.title: Sound, music & audio, The two roads to a talking character
Sound, music & audio, Native vs. designed audio
Directing performance, Two roads to dialogue

diagnoses.diagnosis: The voice and the picture were asked to do each other's jobs. Native-audio generation couples delivery to rendering, when the words must be exact, that coupling breaks.
fix: If the words must be exact, take Road B: generate silent, produce the voice separately, then run a dedicated lip-sync pass that reshapes only the mouth.
Let the voice carry the acting, don't ask the face to do what the voice already does.
For long scenes: generate silent, isolate vocals, post lip-sync. The performance lives in the edit.
Keep a clean dialogue stem, you can revise lines without re-rendering picture.
diagnoses.symptom: Dialogue or audio doesn't match the picture
diagnoses.what_you_see: Mouths move wrong, delivery feels detached from the face, or the exact scripted line never quite lands.

chapters.title: Failure gallery, Failure 2: The live synthetic-performer glitch

diagnoses.diagnosis: Live, unscripted, adversarial settings expose failure modes no rehearsal catches. A synthetic performer with ~2,000 character versions still froze and glitched on live television when asked an unscripted question.
fix: Keep synthetic performers inside edited, controlled contexts, script it, cut it, never let it improvise in public.
If the production needs a synthetic presence, every appearance is pre-rendered and approved.
Interviews and Q&A are the highest-risk setting; treat them as out of scope for synthetic performers.
sources: Tilly Norwood / Piers Morgan Uncensored (kotaku.com, soapcentral.com, filmoria.co.uk)
diagnoses.what_you_see: Freezing, language-switching, or non-sequiturs the moment the setting goes unscripted, the failure no rehearsal catches.
